extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers; college mathematics instructors; curriculum designers
extracted.subtask_description: Conference-proceedings research on undergraduate/college mathematics instruction and students' problem solving behaviors, reporting interventions, observational studies, and microanalyses of mathematicians' embodied practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of worked-out examples (Supplemental Practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplemental Practice (SP) modeled after worked-out example research: students study a worked example for a topic, ask questions about it, then work a similar example without reference to the worked example or other sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the experimental condition SP leaders give worksheets of examples and problems (based on worked-example research) to be completed in groups while assistants circulate to answer questions. The control condition used a student-question-and-answer session rather than a worksheet.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course/instructional structure for intervention
rubrics_metrics.description: Intervention implemented by restructuring the course timetable (two large lectures/week, one active laboratory class, and one Supplemental Practice day dedicated to active group work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design detail matters: SP days, lab class timing, and which students are required or encouraged to attend (initially mandated for low scorers) are part of the intervention fidelity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Random assignment to control and experimental groups
rubrics_metrics.description: One or more course sections are randomly designated as control group(s) and others as experimental group(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Random designation of sections is used to support causal claims about the intervention's effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcome measures (course performance metrics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate impact using quantitative course metrics: total course points, exam scores, individual exam results (e.g., exam 3), quiz scores, final exam, laboratory scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple outcome types should be compared between groups. Disaggregate by assessment type to detect specific effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attendance as moderator (threshold analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Attendance at SP sessions is treated as a moderator: prior analysis showed voluntary attendees of eight or more SP sessions were more successful than those attending fewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include attendance/frequency in analyses (e.g., compare only students with >= 8 SP sessions) to reveal dose–response effects; attendance can substantially change effect sizes and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical significance testing (t-test and p-value thresholds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences between experimental and control groups evaluated with t-tests and reported with p-values (examples: p < 0.05, p < 0.01).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate inferential tests; report exact p-values and indicate which comparisons meet conventional thresholds. Consider multiple comparisons and effect sizes in interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group demographic comparability
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure similar demographics in control and experimental groups to support internal validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report and check demographics; similarity reduces confounding; if imbalanced, adjust analyses or report limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem-solving phases framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Carlson & Bloom's Multidimensional Problem-Solving Framework phases — orientation, planning, executing, and checking — to analyze problem solving activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classify observed student behaviors and inferred mental actions by phase to interpret how reasoning patterns influence each phase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative-reasoning disposition (supporting behaviors)
rubrics_metrics.description: A student propensity to reason about quantities and a problem's context: identifying quantities, relationships, building mental images, and leveraging those throughout problem solving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include drawing and labeling diagrams, revisiting the problem statement to identify goals in terms of quantities, reasoning about relationships before computation, and describing formulas in terms of situational quantities. These behaviors are associated with more meaningful and correct solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/calculation-focused disposition (hindering behaviors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students who focus on recalling procedures and performing calculations (rather than contextual quantitative reasoning) tend to produce less meaningful or incorrect solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed anti-patterns: relying on memory of similar problems, advancing to execution without analyzing meaning, needing numerical results before interpreting them, assigning multiple meanings to numbers, and checking answers by aesthetic plausibility ("not too big" or "not too small").

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of labeled diagrams and explicit identification of known/unknowns
rubrics_metrics.description: When orienting, effective problem solvers frequently draw and label a diagram identifying known and unknown measurements and discuss relationships between quantities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labeling supports planning and monitoring; failure to label is associated with weaker contextual reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planning via reasoning about relationships without immediate computation
rubrics_metrics.description: Good planning involves reasoning about relationships between quantities and mentally simulating (conjecture–imagine–evaluate) solutions without performing numerical operations first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows anticipation of calculations and grounds later computations in quantitative meaning; encourage representing formulas in terms of quantities rather than computing values immediately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring against a mental image (reflective checking)
rubrics_metrics.description: During execution and checking, strong problem solvers monitor calculated values against their mental image of the situation and return to the context to revise if inconsistencies arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitoring based on contextual meaning helps identify incorrect solutions and guides justified revisions; reflective behavior correlates with successful problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical interview methodology for eliciting reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Use structured or semi-structured clinical interviews (with prompts to explain thinking) to reveal reasoning processes that would not appear in written work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical interviews are appropriate for detailed cognitive/process data; they enable inferences about mental actions driving behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open coding qualitative analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze interview data using open coding (Strauss & Corbin) to infer mental actions, categorize behaviors, and relate them to problem solving phases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iteratively generate codes, compare behaviors across subjects, and use coding to identify dispositions and patterns; report coding procedures for transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbol-use as embodied cognition (realms of possibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret mathematicians' symbol-use as embodied: 'realms of possibility' are perceptual anticipations projected onto representation surfaces and defined/bounded by actions (gaps on boards, dividing lines, gestures, gaze, body placement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these constructs to analyze how a mathematician perceives and structures available operations and options; look for physical markers (inscriptions, gestures) that define horizons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paths within and between realms (movement/trajectory indicators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze the 'paths' a mathematician travels within and between realms via gestures, speech, gaze, inscription, and temporal sequences of symbol use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observe sequences where the mathematician changes mode (e.g., steps away to gesture, uses subjunctive language) and how they re-integrate these gestures into inscriptional representations; these indicate navigation of conceptual space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microethnographic microanalysis of video segments
rubrics_metrics.description: Select short (e.g., 2-minute) video segments for detailed microanalysis, alternating individual examinations and collective discussions to generate viable accounts of embodied mathematical practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose segments likely to yield insight, watch repeatedly, generate candidate descriptions rooted in context and subject background, and use team discussion to refine interpretations. This method can broaden perspectives though it may be a case study of a single subject.
